ai.definition: Molecular assemblers are theoretical nanotechnology devices capable of constructing materials, machines, or other structures by manipulating individual atoms or molecules.
ai.howItWorks: These devices would operate through a combination of guided chemical bonding and precise positioning using scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) techniques. The assembler would place atoms in specific positions to form complex structures at the atomic level.
ai.problemSolved: They aim to address limitations in current manufacturing processes by enabling the creation of materials with unprecedented precision, leading to novel applications across various industries including electronics, medicine, and construction.
ai.manufacturing: Currently theoretical; requires breakthroughs in nanoscale manipulation and control technologies.
ai.buildProcess: The exact build process is not yet defined but would involve precise positioning of atoms using advanced STM techniques or similar methods. Theoretical models suggest the use of 'assembly arms' that can manipulate individual molecules.
ai.costDrivers: High development costs, need for cutting-edge materials and equipment, potential energy requirements for atomic manipulation processes.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Long-term potential with significant technical challenges to overcome before practical application.
ai.regulation: No specific regulations currently exist; would require new frameworks addressing safety, environmental impact, and ethical considerations.
ai.risks: Technological feasibility, safety concerns (e.g., accidental release of nanomaterials), economic implications for traditional manufacturing industries.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to early stage of development and potential disruptive nature on existing markets; could revolutionize manufacturing if successful.
ai.futureDevelopment: Continued research in nanotechnology, STM techniques, and molecular self-assembly processes. Potential integration with quantum computing technologies for enhanced precision.

glossary.def: Theoretical nanotechnology devices that can build objects by manipulating individual atoms or molecules.
A high-resolution imaging technique used to visualize surfaces at the atomic level, often proposed for use in molecular assembly processes.

subsystems.name: Probe tips
subsystems.role: atomically sharp needles that pick up, position and bond individual molecules.

subsystems.name: Positioning stage
subsystems.role: holds the tip and workpiece steady to a fraction of an atom's width.

subsystems.name: Reaction site
subsystems.role: where a controlled chemical bond is made or broken on demand.
parts: local energy input (electron, photon or force)

subsystems.name: Feedstock handling
subsystems.role: delivers reactive molecular building blocks to the tip without them reacting anywhere else.

subsystems.name: Sensing and feedback
subsystems.role: detects whether each bond formed correctly.

subsystems.name: Product scaffold
subsystems.role: holds the growing object while more atoms are added and blocks unwanted reactions.

buildSteps.title: Make a workbench
buildSteps.detail: Start with a flat, well-understood surface such as hydrogen-passivated silicon, where single atoms can be added or removed predictably.

buildSteps.title: Sharpen and functionalise probes
buildSteps.detail: Prepare tips ending in a single atom, then attach the molecule that will carry out the chemistry.

buildSteps.title: Build the positioning system
buildSteps.detail: Piezoelectric actuators and heavy acoustic isolation must hold the tip steady to well under a tenth of a nanometre for hours.

buildSteps.title: Demonstrate one reaction
buildSteps.detail: Prove that the tip can reliably place a chosen atom at a chosen site and verify it by imaging — this is the core physics gate.

buildSteps.title: Add error correction
buildSteps.detail: Image each step and undo mistakes, mimicking the proofreading enzymes that biology uses to reach near-perfect accuracy.

buildSteps.title: Parallelise the probes
buildSteps.detail: One tip is far too slow; manufacturing would need thousands of independently controlled tips working at once on the same workpiece.

buildSteps.title: Supply feedstocks
buildSteps.detail: Route reactive intermediates to each tip in a controlled way, so they bond only where intended.

buildSteps.title: Scale to useful objects
buildSteps.detail: Build parts from millions of atoms, then assemble them into macroscopic products.

prerequisites.why: since 1989, scanning probe tips have been able to move individual atoms and place them in patterns.
specific bonds can be made with a tip on certain surfaces, but no general set of reactions and yields has been established.

prerequisites.tech: Parallel probe arrays with individual control
prerequisites.why: throughput is the central obstacle: any practical assembler must place atoms thousands of times faster than a single tip can.
unchecked errors accumulate into defective material, so every placement must be verified and corrected.
molecules reactive enough to be built atom-by-atom are also reactive enough to bond to the wrong places.

pathway.milestone: atom-by-atom manipulation and imaging are routine in a handful of laboratories
pathway.unlocks: proof that positional control of chemistry is physically possible.

pathway.milestone: verified mechanosynthetic reactions with high yield, and short error-corrected chains of building steps
pathway.unlocks: a real, if slow, atomically precise manufacturing method.

pathway.milestone: arrays of thousands of independently driven probes working on one workpiece
pathway.unlocks: throughput high enough to matter outside a laboratory.

pathway.milestone: special-purpose atomically precise manufacturing (for example molecular electronic parts or ultrahard diamond-like materials)
pathway.unlocks: useful products without needing a universal assembler.

pathway.milestone: a general-purpose molecular assembler that can build arbitrary objects from a feedstock
pathway.unlocks: manufacturing limited mainly by design and energy — a claim that is still debated and far from demonstrated.
